cases.title: Security in the workflow
cases.summary: Bring RHEL hardening, CIS checks and audit evidence into a repeatable Ansible and OpenSCAP process.
cases.label: Systems security
paragraphs: My current work includes hardening RHEL 9 servers with Ansible and checking their configuration against CIS benchmarks with OpenSCAP.
Configuration and evidence belong in the same workflow. A repeatable process makes it easier to identify drift, apply approved changes and prepare audit reports.
bullets: Apply approved hardening configuration across servers.
Run compliance scans and retain evidence for review.
Assess application impact before changing authentication, auditing or security controls.
cases.closing: Security changes require the same care as a release: testing, a clear owner, a rollback plan and an understanding of the application.

notes.title: Before the release
notes.summary: A practical checklist for pipeline readiness, verification, ownership and rollback.
paragraphs: A successful pipeline run is one part of a release. The surrounding work matters just as much: agreeing the change, understanding its dependencies and deciding how to respond when verification fails.
Before a change window, review the release scope, configuration, access and dependencies. Name the person responsible for the deployment and the people who can assess application behavior.
bullets: Before deployment: confirm the artifact, configuration, permissions and rollback procedure.
During deployment: watch the pipeline and the service state, with a clear owner for decisions.
After deployment: verify health checks, application behavior, logs and relevant metrics.
Rollback: define the trigger and rehearse the steps before they are needed.
notes.closing: Adapt the checklist to the risk of the system. A small static site and a stateful production application need different levels of verification.

notes.title: Make environments repeatable
notes.summary: How Terraform and Ansible help teams review changes and reduce configuration drift.
paragraphs: Manual configuration leaves an important question unanswered: what exactly changed? Infrastructure as code moves that information into version-controlled files that a team can review.
Reusable Terraform modules help organize infrastructure. Environment-specific values remain explicit, while Ansible can handle configuration and operational tasks where it fits the system.
bullets: Keep reusable structure separate from environment-specific values.
Use pull requests to review infrastructure changes before applying them.
Keep credentials out of source control and use an appropriate secrets mechanism.
Review plans, state access and the expected impact of changes.
Document the process for the person who will operate the environment next.
notes.closing: The goal is an infrastructure setup the team can reproduce and explain. Tool complexity is useful only when it serves that goal.

notes.title: Hardening is a process
notes.summary: Build repeatable checks and audit evidence into the way Linux systems are maintained.
paragraphs: A one-time hardening exercise becomes less useful as a system changes. A repeatable process helps teams understand the current baseline and detect configuration drift.
Start with an agreed baseline and documented exceptions. Ansible can apply approved configuration, while OpenSCAP can assess compliance and produce evidence for review.
bullets: Agree the baseline and exceptions with security and application owners.
Test changes on representative systems before applying them broadly.
Assess the impact of changes to SELinux, authentication, audit rules and services.
Retain scan results and link remediation to reviewed changes.
Repeat checks as the system evolves, rather than treating the first scan as completion.
notes.closing: A useful security process supports availability as well as compliance. Every change needs an owner, verification and a way back.
